newsitem.title: FRANCE: TWA crash investigators to brief French families.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash investigators to brief French families.

text.p: Investigators probing the crash in July of TWA Flight 800 will brief families of French victims in Paris this weekend following complaints that relatives had been left to rely on often contradictory media reports.

A French foreign ministry spokesman said on Wednesday that Robert Francis, vice-chairman of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board and head of the investigation into the crash, would attend the gathering in the French capital.

He said Peter Goels, NTSB spokesman, would also address the meeting for relatives of the 45 French citizens who were among the 230 passengers and crew killed when the Paris-bound Trans World Airlines Boeing 747 exploded shortly after takeoff from New York on July 17.
"The aim of this meeting is to inform the families about the investigation and about support and compensation mechanisms," foreign ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters.
He refused to say when or where it would occur, adding it would be closed to the media.

But relatives and their lawyers told Reuters that the meeting, held under the auspices of France's foreign and justice ministries, would take place on Saturday at the Kleber conference centre near the Champs-Elysee avenue.
They said officials of France's civil aviation authority, U.S. lawyers specialising in airliner crashes and a U.S. victims' association would also attend.
"Since we have come back from New York, the only news we get is when we call the NTSB ourselves," said Herve Schwerts, whose 26-year-old brother-in-law was killed in the crash.
"French authorities have done nothing to pass on news. It's very frustrating to be treated like any old citizen -- we see reports in the press and they're often contradictory," he said.
Paris investigating magistrate Chantal Perdrix has opened a preliminary murder probe into the crash after similar complaints from families of French victims.
The mother of one of the victims said last month that she had been told nothing about any autopsy on her son.
Perdrix was due to meet lawyers and relatives of four of the French victims at the Paris law courts on Wednesday.

"The plaintiffs want to be told the French state is seeking and will seek all the explanations possible for this crash," said a lawyer who declined to be named. He added that the judge was likely to fly to the United States soon.

Relatives of the French victims said they might set up an association with their U.S. counterparts and under the auspices of French authorities -- the foreign and justice ministries, and France's Institute for Support to Victims.
Doutriaux said that French and U.S. officials were in regular contact through respective embassies and that French forensic scientists were taking part in the investigation.

Seeking to counter criticism that Paris had not done enough, the Foreign Ministry said a week after the crash that it had established crisis teams, a hotline, consular officers assigned to families, and legal and psychiatric assistance.
Searchers hunting for debris from the downed flight have found what appears to be part of its centre fuel tank, a critical piece of evidence, officials said on Tuesday.
Investigators maintain there are three possible explanations for the crash -- a bomb, a missile or mechanical failure.
